subject: science
passage: Gardeners have long noticed that plants grown outdoors tend to be shorter and sturdier than those raised indoors. To test whether touch alone could produce this difference, horticulturist Ingrid Halvorsen grew two groups of basil seedlings under identical greenhouse conditions. Once a day, she gently brushed one group with a sheet of cardboard; the other group was left untouched. After four weeks, the brushed seedlings were about 20 percent shorter than the untouched ones, but their stems were thicker, and they bent less when placed in front of a fan.
stem: Based on the text, what did Halvorsen's experiment suggest about basil seedlings?

choices.A: Being touched regularly can make them shorter but sturdier.
choices.B: They grow taller outdoors than they do in a greenhouse.
choices.C: Wind affects their growth more strongly than being touched does.
choices.D: Being brushed daily causes them to produce more leaves.

explanation.why: Halvorsen kept all conditions the same except touch. The brushed seedlings ended up "about 20 percent shorter" with "thicker" stems that "bent less" in front of a fan. So the experiment suggests that touch alone can make seedlings shorter and sturdier.
explanation.A: Correct. The only difference between the groups was brushing, and the brushed plants were shorter with thicker, stiffer stems.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says outdoor plants tend to be shorter, not taller, and the experiment was done entirely in a greenhouse.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The experiment tested touch, not wind; the fan was used only to measure sturdiness afterward.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text never mentions the number of leaves.
